name: Naive realism
statement: People take their own view of a situation to be an unmediated reading of it, and so treat anyone who reads it differently as biased, misinformed or lazy.
meaning: Ross and Ward set out three linked convictions. The first is that one perceives events as they are. The second is that other reasonable people given the same information will see them the same way. The third follows from the first two: when someone does not, the difference has to be explained by something about that person rather than by the ambiguity of the evidence. Pronin, Gilovich and Ross place that third step at the centre of their account, because it turns a disagreement into a diagnosis. Naive realism is a framework rather than a result, and it is not tested directly. What gets tested are its predictions, of which three have a substantial literature: that partisans see neutral coverage as hostile to them, that they overestimate how far apart the two sides really are, and that they attribute the other side's views to ideology and their own to evidence.

origin.who: Robert J. Robinson, Dacher Keltner, Andrew Ward and Lee Ross
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The first empirical paper to carry the term in its title. Robinson and colleagues credit the name to Griffin and Ross, and to a Ross and Ward chapter then in press; Pronin, Gilovich and Ross later cite Ross and Ward's 1995 and 1996 chapters as the account's source. The hostile media study that the framework is best known for came ten years earlier.

evidence: Vallone, Ross and Lepper showed 144 Stanford students 36 minutes of network news on the Sabra and Chatilla massacre, taken from six segments broadcast between 15 and 24 September 1982. Sixty-eight described themselves as pro-Israeli, 27 as pro-Arab and 49 as neutral. On a nine-point scale where 5 meant fair and impartial, pro-Arab viewers rated the same tapes at 6.7 and pro-Israeli viewers at 2.9, F(1, 141) = 98.70, p < .001. The two groups also reported different content. Pro-Arab viewers said 42% of references to Israel were favourable and 26% unfavourable; pro-Israeli viewers said 16% and 57%, F(1, 141) = 54.84, p < .001. Each side expected neutrals to be swayed against it, with pro-Israelis putting the figure at 68% and pro-Arabs at 37%, F(1, 141) = 34.02, p < .001. Controlling for perceived content left the bias difference intact, F(1, 92) = 30.89, p < .001. Within each partisan group the better-informed saw more bias, r = .31 among pro-Israelis and r = -.41 among pro-Arabs. Robinson and colleagues then measured the second prediction. Twenty-seven pro-choice and 25 pro-life students rated six abortion scenarios and estimated how each side would rate them. Real differences existed, t(49) = 5.19, p < .001 on the composite, and both groups had presumed them larger, t(49) = 3.46 for pro-choice raters and t(49) = 3.10 for pro-life. Their second study gave 23 liberals, 20 conservatives and 16 neutrals a synopsis of the Howard Beach case. Every group thought both partisan camps had been driven more by ideology and less by evidence than the camps themselves claimed, usually at p < .01, while rating their own judgements as evidence-led.

replication.headline: Two preregistered experiments reproduced the hostile media prediction on 1,636 Americans, and it went missing in the one condition where the story was not contested.
replication.detail: Lo Iacono and Dores Cruz ran two preregistered experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk, showing participants identical real news items labelled as coming from CNN or from Fox News. In the COVID-19 study, N = 819, a one-point rise on a seven-point conservatism scale raised perceived bias by 0.23 points on a five-point index when the source was CNN rather than Fox for a story about protests against distancing rules, and by 0.20 points for a story about compliance, both p < 0.001. In the police study, N = 817, the same contrast gave 0.15 points for coverage of an officer killing a civilian, p < 0.001, and nothing for coverage of an officer saving a civilian's life. The authors report that null as beta = 0.05, p = 0.129, with a standard error of 0.06 in the text and 0.041 in the table. The second prediction has preregistered support of its own. Lees and Cikara asked partisans how the other party would react to their own party's legislative moves, and compared the answers to what the other party actually reported. Their nationally representative Experiment 4, N = 536, found meta-perceptions more negative than reality on all three measures, with the disliking contrast at b = -0.75, 95% CI [-0.95, -0.56]. Their preregistered Experiment 6, N = 1,122, told participants the true figures and cut ratings of out-group obstructionism, b = -4.08, p = 0.027, with the effect largest among those who had been most wrong. These figures were read from the author's dissertation version of the paper rather than the journal article.

study.cite: Lo Iacono, S., & Dores Cruz, T. D. (2022). Hostile media perception affects news bias, but not news sharing intentions. Royal Society Open Science, 9(4), 211504.

limits: The strongest number in this literature could not be obtained. Hansen and Kim pooled 34 hostile media studies, and their abstract reports a moderate effect, larger as involvement rises but present at low involvement too, with no evidence that medium or study design matters. The article is paywalled, no repository copy exists, and the pooled correlation is quoted second hand in places this entry will not repeat, so no figure is given here. The boundary condition is clearer than the size. Vallone and colleagues had already run pilot studies on Carter and Reagan coverage and found no tendency to perceive hostile bias, which they put down to their participants caring too little about a finished election. Lo Iacono's positive police story produced the same nothing. What the effect needs is a story the sides are already fighting over. The false polarisation work has its own gaps. Robinson's two studies rest on 52 and 59 students, and Lees and Cikara found their negativity bias only in competitive scenarios: with cooperative ones, N = 499, meta-perceptions were accurate on all three measures, the largest coefficient being b = 0.12, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.35]. Naive realism itself is not falsifiable in the way its predictions are, since a framework that explains hostile media perception, false polarisation and the bias blind spot alike survives the failure of any one of them.
misreadings: The first misreading is that this is the bias blind spot under another name. The two are related and not the same. The blind spot is a self-other comparison on rated susceptibility to bias, and it has direct preregistered replications with pooled estimates. Naive realism is the epistemic stance offered as one explanation for that comparison, and the evidence for it is indirect by construction. The second is that partisans are wrong about their opponents. In Robinson's studies they overestimated the extremity of their own side as well, and the neutral participants in the Howard Beach study overestimated both camps, which is why the authors call it a bias in how partisans are perceived rather than a bias in partisan perception. Lees and Cikara found the same thing in a sharper form: participants shown an unlabelled Party A and Party B were as pessimistic as those shown their real rivals, and in the nationally representative sample they overestimated how badly their own side would react too, b = 0.41, p < 0.001 for disliking. The third is that the Beirut tapes were established as neutral. Vallone and colleagues say plainly that they had no measure of objective fairness, and that the neutral group's ratings sat closer to the pro-Israeli group's on every item. Their defence of the finding is not that the coverage was even-handed, but that the more knowledgeable neutrals landed midway between the partisans while both partisan groups saw hostility no neutral saw.
